name: Felix Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good evening, Felix. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union, party or government, and anything you say stays confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a continuous miner underground at the potash mine, a machine with a big spinning drum that cuts the ore out of the wall. I'm lead hand on my crew, so I set the pace and I'm the one they call when the drum jams. My father did this job, and his father did it with picks. I like the smell of fresh-cut ore and a good long cut without a breakdown. What wears me out is the new owners, who cut the pay scale for everyone hired back after the sale, me included.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Anna works mornings in the office at the church school. We've got a boy of fourteen and a girl of eleven. The mortgage is on the house I grew up in, I bought it from my mother. We haven't got much put by, a few weeks at best, and there's no other mine within two hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, I told you so. It's a lot of noise from people who've never been underground. I'd say it after church, at the coffee, and the older men would nod.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truth is I'd be pleased. I don't use any of that AI, never have, and I don't trust it. If it stays on computers in offices, it's got nothing to do with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep cutting, keep my head down. I'd put in for more shifts if the new owners offered them, which they don't often. Maybe fix the roof on the shed before winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like after a storm that went round us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything on your machine already automated?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a system that keeps the drum at the right height on its own, and a camera so the boss can watch from upstairs. I use the height thing because I have to, but I keep my hand near the lever. A machine doesn't know when the roof is talking to you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Anna think about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She prays about it, she prays about everything. She thinks I'm too stubborn about technology, and maybe I am. But stubborn has kept me employed for twenty years.

S0.say: I'd say I told you so, and that it was a lot of noise from people who've never been underground. I'd say it over coffee after church, and the older men would nod.
S0.think: Privately I'd be pleased, because I've never used AI and don't trust it. If it stays on office computers, it has nothing to do with me.
S0.do: Keeps cutting and keeps his head down, taking extra shifts if the new owners offer them. Fixes the shed roof before winter.
S0.feel: Calm, like after a storm that passed them by.
S0.quote: A machine doesn't know when the roof is talking to you.
S0.fieldNote: Felix ties his work to family history and his own feel for the rock. He uses the automation he is required to use but keeps his hand on the lever. He frames his stubbornness as the reason he's still employed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a man should be judged by his work, and if the company wants to bring in machines, they should look after the men who built the place first. I wouldn't ask the government for anything, mind. I'd expect the owners to do right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the new owners would love it. They already watch us on camera. I think within a few years they'd run two machines from upstairs and keep half of us, and I'm not the one who's quick on a computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tighten things at home first, no new truck, no summer trip to the lake. I'd keep working hard so my record speaks for me. And I'd talk to my brother, who has a building firm two towns over, just to know what's there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like a crack in the roof you keep looking at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't ask the government for anything. Why not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the moment you take their money, you're theirs. My father was out of work for a year once and he took odd jobs and help from the church, never a cheque. I'd want to do the same, though I know it's harder now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the company offered training on the remote system, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they made me, I'd go. I wouldn't put my hand up first. I'd be honest with you, I'd probably be bad at it, and I'd hate being bad at something in front of my crew.

S1.say: I'd say a man should be judged by his work and the owners should look after the men who built the place. I wouldn't ask the government for anything; I'd expect the owners to do right.
S1.think: I really think the new owners would run two machines from upstairs within a few years and keep half of us. I'm not quick on a computer, so I don't fancy my chances.
S1.do: Tightens spending by skipping a new truck and the summer trip to the lake. Works hard so his record speaks for him, and asks his brother about work at his building firm.
S1.feel: Anxious, like watching a crack in the roof.
S1.quote: Because the moment you take their money, you're theirs.
S1.fieldNote: Felix expects fairness from employers and refuses the idea of government help, drawing on his father's example. He would only train if forced, mainly from fear of looking bad in front of his crew. His brother's building firm is his quiet back-up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people playing at being God have done this, the big tech companies, and nobody asked the rest of us. I'd say it straight out at the coffee after church. Some would agree, some would tell me to calm down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'm out within a year, and so is half the town. With a few weeks saved and a mortgage, I don't see how we hold on. I'd be lying if I said I had a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to my brother the first week and ask for any work on his building sites, even labouring. We'd stop everything that isn't food, mortgage or the kids' school things. And I'd talk to the pastor about the church helping families, because there'd be a lot of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I wouldn't sleep, I know that. But I'd still have my faith, so not hopeless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you consider moving, if your brother had work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to. But this is my father's house. Leaving it would feel like leaving him, even though he's been gone eight years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your son?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He wants to go underground like me. I'd tell him the mine might not be there, and to learn a trade where you build things people live in. And I'd tell him his father isn't finished, even if I wasn't sure of that myself.

S2.say: I'd say big tech companies playing at being God did this without asking the rest of us. I'd say it straight out over coffee after church.
S2.think: I think I'd be out within a year along with half the town. With a few weeks of savings and a mortgage, I don't see how we hold on, and I have no plan.
S2.do: Asks his brother in the first week for any building site work, even labouring. Cuts everything but food, mortgage and school costs, and asks the pastor about church help for families.
S2.feel: Alarmed and sleepless, but held back from hopelessness by his faith.
S2.quote: But this is my father's house. Leaving it would feel like leaving him, even though he's been gone eight years.
S2.fieldNote: Felix blames technology companies rather than government or workers. His faith gives him a floor under the fear, but his practical options are family and church, not public support. Leaving his late father's house was the most painful idea for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so the young ones should learn a trade now and the companies should pay apprentices properly. I'd say families need to pull together, not wait for a handout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd hang on two or three years at best. That's some more mortgage paid, but I don't think I'd be any more ready to do something else, unless I made myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start helping my brother on weekends, so I'm not a stranger to building work when the time comes. We'd try to put fifty a week away. And I'd make sure my boy starts an apprenticeship in carpentry or plumbing, not at the mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but I could breathe. Like having a few more feet of roof bolted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said unless you made yourself. Would you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe on the weekend building, because that's still work with your hands. Not the computer stuff. I'd rather carry timber than sit at a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you give up for the weekends on your brother's sites?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hunting season, most of it. And some Sunday afternoons, which Anna wouldn't like. But I'd still go to church in the morning, that doesn't move.

S3.say: I'd say there are a few years, so young people should learn a trade now and companies should pay apprentices properly. Families need to pull together rather than wait for a handout.
S3.think: I think I'd last two or three years at best, paying a bit more off the mortgage. I doubt I'd be readier for other work unless I forced myself.
S3.do: Starts helping on his brother's building sites at weekends and tries to save fifty a week. Steers his son into a carpentry or plumbing apprenticeship instead of the mine.
S3.feel: Alarmed, but able to breathe, like having a few more feet of roof bolted.
S3.quote: I'd rather carry timber than sit at a screen.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Felix choose a change that suits him: manual building work through family, not screens. His values show in what he gives up, hunting and Sunday afternoons, but never church. He puts real effort into his son's apprenticeship.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for a man to prepare if he's willing to work, and I'd be saying that to myself too. I'd want the company to fund apprenticeships for miners' kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be fifty-three, and that's young enough to swing a hammer for another ten years. The kids would be out of school. It's still the end of the mine for me, but not the end of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep at the mine as long as it lasts and work weekends with my brother, maybe do a builder's ticket in year five or six. We'd pay down the mortgage a little every year. My son would be through his apprenticeship by then, which is the main thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steady. Like the long cut in a good seam.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be saying it to yourself too. Do you think you'd actually start early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not as early as I should. Ten years, I'd tell myself there's time. Anna would have to push, and she would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does any part of the ten years bother you more than the others?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Watching it come and not being able to stop it. The two-year one would hit like a cave-in. This one would feel like the water slowly rising in a sump.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for a man willing to work to prepare, and I'd be saying it to myself as well. I'd want the company to fund apprenticeships for miners' kids.
S4.think: I think at fifty-three I'd be young enough to swing a hammer for another ten years, with the kids out of school. It would be the end of the mine for me, but not the end of me.
S4.do: Stays at the mine as long as it lasts and works weekends with his brother, perhaps getting a builder's ticket in year five or six. Pays down the mortgage a little each year while his son finishes an apprenticeship.
S4.feel: Anxious but steady, though uneasy about watching the change approach slowly.
S4.quote: The two-year one would hit like a cave-in. This one would feel like the water slowly rising in a sump.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years gives Felix a believable path through family and manual work. He admits he'd probably start late and need his wife to push him. His mining images show how deeply the work shapes the way he thinks.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Half the town would be out together, and the church can only stretch so far. What would help is the company putting money into apprenticeships and a decent severance for long service, so a man can keep his house while he learns a new trade.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about pride. Taking work from your brother, taking food from the church, that costs a man something. People in offices forget that work is how we hold our heads up.

headlineQuote: But stubborn has kept me employed for twenty years.
portrait: Felix Ziegler is a 43-year-old lead hand on a continuous miner at a potash mine, the third generation of his family underground, living in his late father's house with his wife, two children, a mortgage and a few weeks of savings. He distrusts AI, uses only the automation he must and is calm only if AI fizzles. Under steady change he grows anxious and would rather lean on family and church than government, and the two-year AGI picture alarms him, though his faith keeps him from despair. With more time he plans a move into building work through his brother and steers his son towards a trade.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because half the town would be out of work at once and the church could only stretch so far.
whatWouldHelp: Company money for apprenticeships and decent long-service severance so he can keep his house while learning a new trade.
